acts.title: A question, reported in four moves
steps: 1 · Keep the QUESTION WORD. For a yes/no question, use if or whether instead.
2 · Change the PRONOUN, and put the SUBJECT before the verb again.
3 · Drop do / did / does, and step the TENSE back.
4 · No question mark. It is a statement about a question.

“Why are you leaving?” → They asked me ___.
“Can she come?” → I asked ___ come.

acts.title: How to change someone’s mind
text: Everybody has had the experience of arguing with somebody for an hour and changing nothing. The research on persuasion is fairly clear about why, and it is not what most people expect.

A well-known negotiator was once asked what the single most useful skill in his work was. He did not say confidence, and he did not say argument. He said listening. When he was asked whether he meant listening politely while waiting to speak, he said no — he meant asking questions until you understand what actually matters to the other person, which is almost never the thing they are arguing about.

Psychologists who study the subject describe the same pattern. In one study, participants were asked how well they could explain a policy they supported. Most said very well. They were then asked to explain it in detail, step by step. Afterwards they were asked the same question again, and their confidence had dropped sharply. Nobody had argued with them. They had simply discovered how little they knew.

The second finding is about names and attention. One book on persuasion devotes a whole chapter to remembering people’s names: look at the face, use the name in the conversation, write it down afterwards. It sounds trivial. It works because it is evidence that you were paying attention, and people rarely change their minds for somebody who was not.

None of this is quick. Everybody wants to know whether there is a phrase that wins an argument. There is not. What there is, is a much slower method: find out what the objection really is, and answer that.

items.s: The negotiator said confidence was his most useful skill.
He meant listening in order to find out what really matters to the other person.

tts: So, you’ve been reading our book of the week, How to Persuade and Influence People. Did you enjoy it?
Yes, actually. I thought it might be useful, but I didn’t really expect to enjoy reading it. It was quite entertaining.
So what did you actually learn from reading it?
There were some very useful tips for remembering people’s names. He says that’s important in getting people to trust you.
To listen carefully when the person first says their name, to use their name in the conversation, to look at their face and associate it with the name, and to write it down afterwards.
And what does the book say about persuading people?
Probably the most important thing is to really listen, and to ask questions to find out what matters to them.
So, most important question: are you better at persuading people now?
I’m not sure. Ask me again in a few months.

write.q: Write about a conversation where somebody asked you a lot of questions — an interview, a first meeting, a difficult discussion. Report at least four of the questions and two of the answers. Watch the word order: a reported question is not a question.
write.model:
Last month I sat on the other side of an interview for the first time, and I found it much harder than I expected.

My colleague asked the candidate why she had left her previous job after eleven months, which I would never have dared to ask. She then wanted to know whether the decision had been hers. The candidate said it had not been, and explained that the whole department had been closed. My colleague asked what she had done in the six months since, and she admitted that she had done almost nothing for the first two.

I asked one question and it was a bad one. I asked her where she saw herself in five years, and she told me, politely, that nobody had ever answered that honestly.

Afterwards I wondered how many good candidates we lose because of questions like mine.

speak.q: Report a real conversation out loud: three questions somebody asked you and how you answered. Then say what you wondered afterwards.
speak.model: At the interview she asked me why I had applied twice, and I said the first time I hadn’t been ready. She wanted to know whether anything had changed since, which was fair. Then she asked what I would do in my first week, and I told her I would spend it listening. Afterwards I wondered why nobody had asked me a single question about the software.
